methodological_rigor.justification: The study integrates ctDNA analysis, tissue WES, bulk RNA-seq, Ba/F3 cellular models with site-directed mutagenesis, PDX in vivo experiments (n=6 per group), and structural modeling to characterize resistance to lirafugratinib. The comparison of resistance mutation spectra to lirafugratinib vs. futibatinib using an appropriate permutation test (P<1×10-5) is methodologically sound. The PDX models use direct patient-derived material with relevant mutations. Three patients treated with the proposed sequential strategy provide clinical proof-of-concept. Key limitations: small cohort (n=30 total, n=16 with acquired resistance), three different liquid biopsy panels with varying sensitivity thresholds, Mycoplasma testing not performed on Ba/F3 cells, and GSEA analyses are explicitly noted as underpowered. PDX models contain only one FGFR2 mutation, not recapitulating polyclonal resistance.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a case series within a phase I/II clinical trial (ReFocus) combined with preclinical validation, mapping to LoE 4. The clinical relevance is high: FGFR2-driven cancers (particularly cholangiocarcinoma) are an area of active treatment development with approved agents. The identification of recurrent M538I/L618F resistance mutations in 69% of acquired-resistance cases and the demonstration of futibatinib activity against these mutations in vitro, in vivo, and in three clinical cases directly inform treatment sequencing decisions. As lirafugratinib awaits approval (2026-2027), these findings will immediately guide clinical practice.

reporting_quality.justification: The study follows precision oncology reporting conventions: patients are characterized by FGFR2 alteration type, prior treatment, and response; resistance mutations are systematically tabulated with VAF data; individual patient clinical courses are depicted with longitudinal ctDNA and imaging data. The definition of primary vs. acquired resistance is explicit. The allelic status of co-occurring mutations is assessed where feasible. Structural modeling uses published PDB coordinates with Maestro. Limitations (three liquid biopsy panels, missing WES/RNA-seq in some cases) are transparently acknowledged. Raw sequencing data availability is not stated.

novelty_literature.justification: This is the first comprehensive characterization of resistance to lirafugratinib, identifying M538I and L618F as the dominant (69%) acquired resistance mutations—a pattern distinct from futibatinib resistance (N550/V565-enriched). The complementarity of the two irreversible FGFR inhibitors and the proposed sequencing strategy based on mutation profiling is a novel and actionable clinical framework. The structural analysis explaining why lirafugratinib is sensitive to M538I/L618F while futibatinib is not (due to different binding conformations and interaction networks) provides mechanistic depth beyond prior pharmacologic descriptions.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well-organized with clear sections addressing primary resistance, acquired resistance, complementarity analysis, structural biology, and clinical sequencing evidence. Clinical case descriptions are informative and appropriately detailed. The proposed treatment decision algorithm in Figure 6 effectively communicates the practical implications. The discussion acknowledges all major limitations transparently. The writing is precise and appropriate for a precision oncology audience.

key_strengths: First systematic characterization of lirafugratinib resistance, identifying M538I/L618F as dominant (69%) acquired resistance mutations complementary to futibatinib's N550/V565 resistance spectrum
Integrated multi-platform approach: ctDNA/WES for resistance characterization, Ba/F3 cellular models, PDX in vivo validation, structural analysis, and clinical proof-of-concept cases
Statistically rigorous comparison of mutation spectra between lirafugratinib and futibatinib using permutation testing (P<1×10-5), demonstrating complementarity

Immediately actionable clinical framework: mutation-guided FGFR inhibitor sequencing strategy supported by preclinical and clinical evidence with direct regulatory timing (lirafugratinib approval 2026-2027)
key_concerns: Small cohort (n=30 total; n=16 with acquired resistance) limits statistical confidence and precludes analysis by tumor type and FGFR2 alteration subtype
Only three patients received the proposed lirafugratinib-futibatinib sequence, and all had intervening chemotherapy; direct sequential switching without interval treatment is unvalidated
Three liquid biopsy panels with different sensitivity thresholds introduce technical variability; Mycoplasma testing was not performed on Ba/F3 cells
Genetic resistance mechanisms only; lineage plasticity, epigenetic, and microenvironmental resistance mechanisms are not assessed
chief_reviewer.rationale: This translational precision oncology study provides novel, clinically actionable insights into lirafugratinib resistance patterns and the rationale for FGFR inhibitor sequencing, supported by integrated preclinical and early clinical evidence; Tier 2 placement is merited by the mechanistic depth, regulatory timing relevance, and multi-platform validation, with minor revisions to address data sharing and to clarify the limitations of the three-patient clinical validation.
